articles.title: Republicans experience worse mental health in Democratic neighborhoods, study finds
articles.summary: A large national study finds that Republicans living in heavily Democratic neighborhoods report higher rates of anxiety, depression, and loneliness. Democrats, however, show similar mental health regardless of their neighborhood's political makeup.

articles.title: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
articles.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.

articles.title: Family ties emerge as a key link between poverty and teen well-being in Taiwanese study
articles.summary: Among more than 1,300 Taiwanese adolescents living in poverty, those facing more material hardship reported poorer family relationships and more psychological distress. Family ties appeared to be the most consistent link between deprivation and adolescents’ well-being.

articles.title: Psychologists map the connection between dark personality traits and romantic jealousy
articles.summary: New psychological research reveals how aggressive personality traits are channeled into romantic jealousy. The findings suggest that hostility often expresses itself through an obsessive, possessive approach to love, acting as a bridge to severe jealousy.

articles.title: Brain differences in dyslexia appear before children learn to read
articles.summary: Children who go on to develop dyslexia already show weaker brain responses to repeated written words in kindergarten, before formal reading lessons start. Their responses to faces, houses, and objects look much like those of their peers.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: New study finds children and teens reason differently about participation trophies
articles.summary: Adults argue endlessly about participation trophies. A new study asked the people who actually receive them, finding that children as young as 7 expect winner-only awards to boost effort, while teenagers also expect them to encourage cheating.

articles.title: The right message can shift support for universal basic income across party lines
articles.summary: Support for universal basic income looks like a straightforward partisan split. But a new study of more than 2,000 Americans suggests that personal values about equality and tradition do more to shape reactions than party labels.

articles.title: Steroid users face triple the risk of long-term erectile dysfunction
articles.summary: Men who use anabolic steroids to build muscle face a substantially higher risk of long-term erectile dysfunction. A new study shows that even years after starting the drugs, steroid users are three times more likely to require impotence medication.

articles.title: Common genetic variants matter more in Alzheimer’s than scientists thought
articles.summary: Some researchers had argued that the hunt for common Alzheimer’s risk genes was nearly finished. A new study of 2.8 million people found 48 previously unknown risk regions and nearly tripled estimates of how much common variants contribute.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
articles.summary: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

articles.summary: Every group effort seems to benefit from a few people who always pitch in. A new mathematical model suggests those reliable contributors make collective action easier to start, but can also give everyone else an excuse to coast.

articles.title: Popular cannabis supplement shows inconsistent anti-inflammatory effects in brain cells
articles.summary: Cannabigerol, a non-intoxicating cannabis compound sold as a supplement, is often promoted as anti-inflammatory. A new laboratory study found its effects on brain immune cells were inconsistent, and that most doses broke isolated DNA strands.

articles.summary: Humiliation can leave memories that are hard to shake. A new study suggests that people who have felt humiliated tend to be less happy, and that repetitive negative thinking may be part of the reason.

articles.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
articles.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

articles.title: New case study offers causal evidence linking the right amygdala to PTSD
articles.summary: A man with epilepsy and severe PTSD had part of his right amygdala inactivated during awake surgery. Within 20 minutes, he stopped reading ambiguous faces as fearful. Two months later, his PTSD score had fallen below the diagnostic threshold.

articles.title: People tend to underestimate how much they get in the way of their partner’s goals
articles.summary: In a 14-day diary study of 106 cohabiting couples, people were accurate, on average, about how much they helped their partner’s goals but tended to underestimate how much they got in the way.
